correctness.rationale: The first monoid consists of the six units, a three-element left-zero ideal above zero on which the units act by conjugating transpositions on the left and trivially on the right, and zero. For an identity-preserving second map, an automorphic restriction to the units forces the image of zero to be zero and allows either collapse of the three singular idempotents to zero or their unique equivariant permutation (six maps of each rank 7 and 10). A restriction onto an order-two subgroup collapses the three idempotents to a common value, either zero or the singular idempotent fixed by that subgroup. The zero image then gives, per subgroup, two rank-3 maps and one rank-4 map. A trivial restriction maps the three singular idempotents to a common idempotent d and zero to any q satisfying dq=qd=q, giving one rank-1, eight rank-2 and three rank-3 maps. For a nonunital map, the local monoid of the image of 1 is either {0} or {0,t_s}, giving four constants and six rank-2 maps in all. Thus there are 33 unital and ten nonunital maps; the combined rank multiplicities at 1,2,3,4,7,10 are 5,14,9,3,6,6. The frozen checker was inspected without execution; independent reconstruction of the permutation table and exhaustive locally constrained homomorphisms was run successfully with python3 /workspace/branches/s3_independent_replay.py. The six full-rank maps are automorphisms of E1. If the wording about automorphisms of E2 is read literally as Aut(E2), the independent replay also verifies cardinality six: fixing each unit leaves all 43 elements distinguishable by invariant multiplication signatures, and the six inner automorphisms realize the six restrictions on the unit group. No assertion about later tower levels is tested.

value.rationale: S3 is the first nonabelian symmetric degree and lies outside the motivating large-degree classification. A complete second-tower image-rank census, with the unital/nonunital split, supplies a natural exceptional-degree benchmark and shows which ranks are possible, not just the size of a routine Cayley table.
